tasks.extracted: Seven studies met the criteria. Against lifetime abstainers, ischaemic heart disease (deaths and new cases combined) in people averaging under 30 g a day without heavy drinking occasions: relative risk 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71, printed identically in the abstract and the results); with heavy drinking occasions: 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37). Editors' calculation: the geometric midpoint of 0.53 to 0.71 is 0.61, so the point estimate or one limit is probably misprinted.

tasks.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4203905 (BMC Medicine 2014;12:182), as read for card sc_roerecke_2014: all sections; Additional file 1 not read
tasks.extracted: No long-term randomized studies of alcohol and ischaemic heart disease exist; short-term studies show dose-dependent effects on surrogate markers (higher HDL cholesterol, less platelet activation, lower fibrinogen, anti-inflammatory effects), and HDL cholesterol is also raised by regular heavy drinking and is highest in people with alcohol use disorder. The authors set aside the ADH1B Mendelian randomization study (Holmes et al., 2014), which concluded there was no protective effect, as hard to compare with the epidemiology because the variant was also linked to less binge drinking.

tasks.extracted: Relative risk with against without heavy drinking occasions, at the same average intake under 30 g a day: 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), higher than the 1.45 of the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; the authors read this as the effect of episodic heavy drinking being greatest at low average intake. How the ratio and its interval were obtained is not described; editors' arithmetic: 1.12 divided by 0.64 is 1.75, and the two estimates share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within studies.
